clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by biallelic variants in SCARB2, which encodes the lysosomal membrane protein LIMP-2
Presents in adolescence or early adulthood with progressive action and stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, tremor, and later generalised seizures and ataxia
A defining feature is coexisting proteinuric renal disease, typically focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which may precede, accompany, or follow the neurological features
The renal and neurological components can present years apart, so a history of unexplained proteinuria in a patient with myoclonus is an important clue
LIMP-2 is the receptor that traffics beta-glucocerebrosidase to the lysosome, so the disorder mechanistically overlaps lysosomal biology
Some patients develop sensorineural hearing loss
Cognition is usually relatively preserved despite disabling motor features
Management is supportive: antimyoclonic and antiseizure therapy plus nephrology care, with renal replacement or transplantation as renal failure advances
reference.pathophysiology: Action myoclonus-renal failure syndrome results from loss-of-function variants in SCARB2, encoding the lysosomal integral membrane protein 2 (LIMP-2). LIMP-2 serves as the sorting receptor that escorts beta-glucocerebrosidase from the endoplasmic reticulum to the lysosome and also maintains lysosomal membrane integrity. Its deficiency impairs lysosomal function in neurons and podocytes. In the nervous system this produces a progressive myoclonic phenotype with cortical hyperexcitability, while in the kidney it disrupts podocyte function, causing proteinuria and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis that can progress to renal failure. The shared reliance of brain and glomerulus on intact lysosomal membrane biology explains the otherwise unusual pairing of neurological and renal disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other progressive myoclonus epilepsies (Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora disease, sialidosis)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (early, before renal disease apparent)
Other genetic causes of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria, with renal function tests
Electroencephalography and neurophysiology for cortical myoclonus
Renal biopsy where glomerular disease requires characterisation
Brain MRI to exclude alternative structural causes
redFlags: Progressive renal impairment heralding end-stage kidney disease
Status myoclonicus or worsening seizure control
Rapid loss of ambulation from disabling action myoclonus
reference.prognosis: A progressive disorder; neurological disability accrues over years and renal disease often advances to end-stage kidney failure, though renal replacement therapy and transplantation can be undertaken.
pitfalls: Treating the myoclonus in isolation and missing coexisting renal disease, or vice versa
Failing to screen for proteinuria in a young patient with progressive myoclonus
Confusing the phenotype with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and delaying genetic testing
Overlooking that renal and neurological onset may be separated by years
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Symptomatic control of cortical myoclonus and seizures with agents such as valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam or piracetam, avoiding aggravating sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine and phenytoin
Management of proteinuric focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with renin-angiotensin system blockade under nephrology co-care
Renal replacement therapy by dialysis, and consideration of kidney transplantation, for progression to end-stage kidney failure
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and mobility and communication aids for progressive myoclonus and ataxia
Audiometric monitoring and hearing support for associated sensorineural hearing loss
Coordinated multidisciplinary neurology and nephrology follow-up given the years-apart evolution of the two components
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive SCARB2 inheritance, with family screening
